title: Limits and the Watchdog: Failing Into a Safe State

questions.question: Your control program stops running while the motor command is 0.9. What happens?
options: The motor ramps down slowly on its own
The motor keeps running at 0.9 until something physical stops it
The motor stops, because no new command arrives
The operating system resets the motor to zero
questions.explanation: Nothing tells the actuator that the sender died. The last command it received stays in effect, which is why commands need an expiry.

questions.question: What does feeding a watchdog mean?
options: Recording that a fresh command arrived, which pushes the expiry deadline out
Setting the output to the safe value
Restarting the control loop
Increasing the timeout
questions.explanation: Each feed says the sender is still alive. If feeding stops, the deadline passes and the guard forces the safe value.

questions.question: Why must a watchdog that has never been fed report expired?
options: Because zero is not a valid time
To make the first feed take effect immediately
Because the timeout has not been set yet
Otherwise it hides the worst case, where commands never arrived at all
questions.explanation: Starting in a trusting state means a robot whose command source never started would run on stale defaults with nothing objecting.

questions.question: Why does the safe value have no default in this design?
options: The safe state depends on the machine, and a silent default hides a safety decision
To force the caller to write more code
Because C++ does not allow default arguments in constructors
Because zero is unsafe for all machines
questions.explanation: Zero is safe for a wheel and dangerous for an arm holding a load. Requiring the value makes the engineer make that decision knowingly.

questions.question: What can a software watchdog inside your control program NOT protect against?
options: A stalled control loop
A command source that never starts
Its own process being killed
A thread that stops calling update
questions.explanation: It disappears with the process it lives in. That is why a hardware watchdog in the drive and a wired emergency stop sit outside it.

questions.question: Why is an emergency stop wired so that a broken wire stops the machine?
options: Because it uses less current
So a failure in the safety circuit itself results in a stop rather than an unnoticed loss of protection
Because normally open contacts are more expensive
So the stop button can be pressed remotely
questions.explanation: The principle is that the failure of the protection must itself be safe. Phase 19 covers this and the standards that require it.
